message.content: 獅子（屬於貓科）與斑馬（屬於馬科）雖然都屬於哺乳類，但它們在進化樹上相距甚遠。兩者最後一次共用的祖先大約生活在白堊紀晚期，距今約七千五百萬至八千萬年前，屬於「拉魯西亞獸綱」（Laurasiatheria）的一個早期小型、食性多樣的哺乳動物。這個祖先在之後分化成了現今所見的食肉目（Carnivora）和奇蹄目（Perissodactyla），最終演化出今天的獅子和斑馬。
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "獅子和斑馬的共同祖先是什麼？" which translates to "What is the common ancestor of lions and zebras?" They want an answer about the evolutionary relationship between lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus zebra). The question likely expects a discussion of their common ancestor in terms of taxonomy: both belong to the order Carnivora? Wait, zebras are equids, order Perissodactyla. Lions are felids, order Carnivora. So they diverged earlier. Their common ancestor would be a mammalian ancestor from the Eutheria clade, maybe within the clade of placental mammals. But more specifically, the last common ancestor of the families Felidae (cats) and Equidae (horses) would be a member of the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually, Felidae is part of the suborder Feliformia within Carnivora, while Equidae is part of Perissodactyla. Both are within the clade of Laurasiatheria? Let's recall: Laurasiatheria includes orders like Artiodactyla, Perissodactyla, Chiroptera, Cetartiodactyla, etc. Carnivora is also part of Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of Felidae and Equidae would be within Laurasiatheria, perhaps within the clade of the group that gave rise to the orders of Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That ancestor would have lived around 70-80 million years ago. The last common ancestor of all placental mammals is older (~100-120 million years ago). But the question might be answered simply: "They share a common ancestor that lived around 70 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria." Or "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, early mammal that lived during the Paleocene epoch."

We can provide a concise answer: "Lions (family Felidae) and zebras (family Equidae) diverged from a common ancestor that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, belonging to the clade Laurasiatheria." We can mention that this ancestor was a small, omnivorous mammal.
